paragraphs: When the chazan repeats the Amidah, the congregation must be silent and direct their attention to the berachot that the chazan recites, and answer Amen. If there are not nine people directing their attention to his berachot, his berachot are close to being in vain. So it is written in the book "Olat Tamid," in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah, of blessed memory, that if there are not ten people directing their attention, the berachah becomes a berachah levatalah (a blessing said in vain). And if each person says, "surely there are ten others besides me [paying attention]," then not even a single person will actually be attentive — rather, on the contrary, each person must say the opposite, "there are not ten others besides me," [and take responsibility upon himself]. Therefore the chazanim must raise their voices throughout the repetition, from beginning to end, and not be like those who raise their voice only at the very end of the closing berachah, for the congregation must hear all the words of the prayer from beginning to end without any omission. And a chazan whose voice is low, where there is a strong presumption that those far from him who sit at the back of the synagogue will certainly not hear his voice properly, the beit din must remove him. And those who appoint a chazan with a low voice bear the sin of the congregation upon their necks. For one whose voice is naturally low — when it happens that his voice deteriorates occasionally, from any of the various causes that are always present — such a person's voice will certainly not be heard beyond four amot.

clarification.explanation: During the chazan's repetition the congregation must be silent and direct their attention to his berachot and answer Amen; if there are not nine people directing their attention to his berachot, his berachah is close to being in vain. He warns that no one should say to himself, "surely there are nine others directing their attention besides me," for if everyone thinks this way, not even a single person will actually be attentive in practice — rather, on the contrary, each person must be concerned and say to himself, "there are not nine others besides me," and take the intention upon himself seriously. Therefore the chazanim must raise their voice throughout the entire repetition (not only at the end), so that the congregation hears everything. A chazan whose voice is too weak (such that those sitting far away cannot hear) must be replaced by the beit din; and those who appoint such a chazan bear the responsibility.
takeaways: The chazan's repetition requires a raised voice throughout, so that the congregation can hear, direct their attention, and answer Amen.

One should not rely on the assumption that "surely there are nine others directing their attention" — rather, one should assume that he himself must direct his attention, since otherwise no one might do so.
A chazan whose voice is too weak must be replaced.

paragraphs: Even though the simple reason for the repetition is to discharge the obligation for one who is not proficient [in prayer], this is not the primary reason, for in our time this reason has almost become obsolete, since everyone prays from siddurim, and one who prays by heart is [already] proficient. And if there is someone completely unlearned, he stands like a stone and the repetition does not help him, since he pays no attention to it, as he understands nothing at all. But in truth, the primary reason for the repetition is explained in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, according to the esoteric tradition, and explained in Sefer HaKavanot: that during the repetition of the prayer, all the same rectifications that were performed during the silent Amidah are performed again — except that the repetition reaches a higher and more elevated place than the place reached by the silent prayer. This is the reason that the silent prayer must be said very carefully in a whisper, and the Zohar was very strict about one who raises his voice in his prayer, out of fear that the kelipot might attach themselves to it. But the repetition, being in a higher and more elevated place, has no attachment for the kelipot there, and therefore it is said aloud without fear. Accordingly, from these two points you can understand the greatness of the repetition: first, that it is said aloud; and second, that permission was not given for an individual to repeat the prayer, but only for a congregation of ten. Therefore the repetition should never be omitted at all, except in a time of pressing need when no time remains, or when there are exactly ten [and no more], and it is clear to him that among them there are common people who pay no attention to the repetition, and would not pay attention to answer even for the sake of [becoming] craftsmen — in such a case the chazan should recite the first three berachot aloud together with the congregation while they pray silently, so as to be able to say the Kedushah of "Nakdishach Venaaritzach," and after the closing of "Atah Kadosh" the chazan too should finish the prayer silently. See "Minchat Aharon," Klal 16, letter 56, regarding this custom; see there.

clarification.explanation: The simple reason for the chazan's repetition (to discharge the obligation for one who is not proficient) is nearly irrelevant nowadays, since everyone prays from a siddur. The primary reason (according to the esoteric tradition) is that during the repetition all the rectifications of the silent prayer are performed again, but in a higher and more elevated place; therefore in the silent prayer one is very careful to say it quietly (out of concern for the attachment of the kelipot), whereas in the repetition, where the kelipot have no attachment, it is said aloud and without fear. From this it follows that the repetition should never be omitted at all, except in a time of great pressing need (no time remains, or the minyan is barely met and most of the people have no intention of answering at all) — in which case the chazan says the first three berachot aloud with the congregation (in order to say the Kedushah), and from "Atah Kadosh" onward he too continues silently.
takeaways: The true reason for the chazan's repetition (according to the esoteric tradition): the rectifications return and are elevated to a higher place, where there is no fear of the kelipot, and therefore it is said aloud.
The repetition should never be omitted except in a time of great pressing need, in which case at least the first three berachot and the Kedushah are said.

paragraphs: Before the Kedushah of "Nakdishach," a person should intend to fulfill this positive commandment that we were commanded in the verse "And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel" (Vayikra 22:32), which the holy Zohar explained to mean that we are obligated to sanctify His blessed Name through the mystical secret of the Kedushah of "Nakdishach Venaaritzach." And when he says "The whole earth is full of His glory," he should intend that "the earth" refers to the sefirah of Malchut, which is called "eretz" (earth), and he should intend to include himself within Malchut, in order to receive holiness from the holiness that is drawn down to Malchut when we recite this order of Kedushah — for we, the children of Malchut, receive holiness through our "mother" Malchut. All of this he should intend when saying "The whole earth is full of His glory," as mentioned in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar HaKavanot; see there.

clarification.explanation: Before the Kedushah of "Nakdishach," a person should intend to fulfill the positive commandment that we were commanded in the verse "And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel" — which the holy Zohar explained to mean that we are obligated to sanctify His blessed Name through the mystical secret of the Kedushah of "Nakdishach Venaaritzach." And when he says "The whole earth is full of His glory," he should intend that "the earth" refers to the sefirah of Malchut (called "eretz"), and intend to include himself within Malchut in order to receive holiness from the holiness drawn down to it in reciting this order of Kedushah — for we, the children of Malchut, receive holiness through our "mother" Malchut. All of this he should intend when saying "The whole earth is full of His glory" (as taught by the Ari in Sha'ar HaKavanot).
takeaways: Before "Nakdishach," one should intend to fulfill the commandment "And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel" — to sanctify God's Name through the Kedushah.
In "The whole earth is full of His glory," one should intend that "earth" refers to the sefirah of Malchut, and include himself within it in order to receive the holiness drawn down to it.

paragraphs: When the chazan reaches "Nakdishach," a person must step back three steps forward, to the place where he stood while praying the silent Amidah, and close his eyes with complete intention. He should also be very careful to align his feet during the Kedushah, in the mystical secret of "and their feet were a straight foot" (Yechezkel 1:7), and he should say together with the chazan from "Nakdishach Venaaritzach" until the conclusion of the entire Kedushah. However, the two words "Nakdishach Venaaritzach" he should say aloud, and the rest in a whisper; and only the verses "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh, etc.," "Baruch, etc.," and "Yimloch, etc." he should say aloud, with closed eyes, and with an upward leap (dillug), as mentioned in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar HaKavanot. And know that although the Rabbi [author of] "Mishnat Chassidim," of blessed memory, wrote, according to the esoteric tradition, that the leap applies only to the verse "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" and not to "Baruch" and "Yimloch," the custom, as written by the Gaon the Shelah, of blessed memory, is to leap during "Baruch" and "Yimloch" as well, three times; see "Minchat Aharon," Klal 16, letter 29; see there — and so we practice.

clarification.explanation: When the chazan reaches "Nakdishach," one takes three steps forward (back to the place where he stood during the silent Amidah), closes his eyes with intention, aligns his feet (the mystical secret of "a straight foot"), and says the whole Kedushah together with the chazan — with "Nakdishach Venaaritzach" aloud and the rest in a whisper, and the verses "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh," "Baruch," and "Yimloch" aloud, with eyes closed, with an upward leap. The Rabbi "Mishnat Chassidim" wrote, according to the esoteric tradition, that the leap belongs only to the verse "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" and not to "Baruch" and "Yimloch," but the accepted custom (as ruled by the Gaon the Shelah, and so we practice) is to leap during "Baruch" and "Yimloch" as well — in all three verses.
takeaways: During the Kedushah: one takes three steps forward, closes his eyes, and leaps upward at the three verses of the Kedushah (Kadosh, Baruch, Yimloch).

Some disagree ("Mishnat Chassidim") that the leap belongs only to "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" and not to "Baruch/Yimloch," but the prevailing custom (the Shelah, and so we practice) is to leap at all three.

paragraphs: It is written in Sefer Heichalot that the Holy One, blessed be He, said: "I have no pleasure in the world except at the time when My children sanctify Me and say 'Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh,' with their eyes lifted upward and raising themselves upward." And I explained, with the help of Heaven, in my sermons, what is meant by "I have no pleasure (hana'ah) in the world" — that is, [a wordplay reading it as] "Hei na'ah" (a beautiful Hei), for through the recitation of the Kedushah, holiness is drawn down to Malchut, which is the final Hei of the [divine] Name, as I wrote above in the name of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, regarding the intention of "The whole earth is full of His glory." And it is written in "Chesed LaAlafim" that when saying "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh," one should leap upward three times, with eyes closed and lifted upward; and when saying "Baruch, etc.," one should bow and straighten up at the [divine] Name, and leap once, with eyes lifted upward; and likewise when saying "Yimloch," one should bow and straighten up at the Name, and leap, and remain standing there in place with feet aligned and joined together until answering Amen to "Ha'El HaKadosh." This is the order of the Kedushah, to sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and the God of Israel — until here his words. Now, this bowing and straightening mentioned there is not mentioned in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory. And I asked the Rabbi, the Gaon, our teacher Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, may he live long, about the custom of the devout ones of "Beit El" [yeshiva], may it be built and established, in the holy city of Jerusalem, and he wrote that they do not practice this, but say them without bowing and straightening. And indeed here in our city too, we do not practice bowing and straightening, but only perform the leap specifically.

clarification.explanation: It is brought from Sefer Heichalot that the Holy One, blessed be He, derives pleasure from Israel's sanctification, "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh," when their eyes are lifted upward. The explanation (according to the esoteric tradition): reciting the Kedushah draws holiness down to the attribute of Malchut (the final Hei of the divine Name). In saying "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" one leaps upward three times with eyes closed and lifted; in "Baruch" and "Yimloch" — the custom in Baghdad (and likewise in Jerusalem) is to leap only, without the bowing and straightening practiced elsewhere. And at the end one leaps and remains standing in place, feet aligned and joined, until answering Amen to "Ha'El HaKadosh."
takeaways: The custom of Baghdad (and Jerusalem): leaping only during Kadosh-Baruch-Yimloch, without bowing and straightening.

paragraphs: The leap consists of raising one's heels and body upward, and one should not leap excessively, lest people mock him, as mentioned in the book "Kesher Godel." And the three leaps of "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" — each elevation should be slightly higher than the previous one, for "one ascends in holiness," as mentioned by the Acharonim; see "Kaf HaChaim." And if an individual heard the Kedushah in the middle of his own prayer, at a point where he cannot answer the Kedushah, he should not perform the leaps together with the congregation, even silently, but rather stand still and be silent, directing his attention to the chazan in order to hear it from him.

clarification.explanation: The leap is the raising of one's heels and body upward, without exaggeration that would lead to mockery. The three leaps of "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" — each leap slightly higher than the previous one ("one ascends in holiness"). An individual who heard the Kedushah in the middle of his own prayer, at a point where he cannot answer, should not leap together with the congregation even silently, but rather stand still, be silent, and direct his attention to listen.
takeaways: The leaps of the Kedushah rise gradually; an individual who cannot actually answer should not leap, but only stand silently and direct his attention.

paragraphs: An individual who was praying, and when he reached the point of Kedushah [in his own prayer] the congregation was saying the Kedushah of "U'va LeTzion" or the Kedushah of Yotzer, is not permitted to say "Kadosh, etc." together with them, since the Kedushot are not equivalent. Likewise, if he is praying Shacharit and hears the Kedushah of Musaf, he does not answer with them when he reaches the point of Kedushah [in his own prayer], as Rabbi "Peri Chadash," of blessed memory, wrote. And even though the Rema, of blessed memory, wrote that in this case he should answer, [the principle that] "sit and do nothing" is preferable [applies here].

clarification.explanation: An individual who is praying and hears a Kedushah different from his own (for example, the Kedushah of "U'va LeTzion" while he is still in Shacharit) does not answer with them, since the Kedushot are not equivalent (and likewise Shacharit versus Musaf); "sit and do nothing" is preferable.
takeaways: One does not answer a Kedushah different from the one he is currently in during his own prayer (for example, the Kedushah of Musaf while he is still praying Shacharit).

paragraphs: One should not answer "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" until the chazan finishes the word "Ve'amar"; and likewise "Baruch" until he says the word "Ve'omrim"; and likewise "Yimloch" until he says "Leimor" — for if one answers before he finishes, it is considered like an "amen chatufah" (a snatched, premature Amen), as mentioned in Sefer Chassidim, whose words are cited by the Acharonim, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: One should not answer "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" until the chazan finishes the word "Ve'amar," nor "Baruch" until "Ve'omrim," nor "Yimloch" until "Leimor" — otherwise it is like a premature, "snatched" Amen.
takeaways: One answers each verse of the Kedushah only after the chazan has finished his introductory word (Ve'amar/Ve'omrim/Leimor).

paragraphs: An individual who was praying, and when he reached the point of Kedushah did not hear "Nakdishach" from the chazan, but only heard the congregation answering "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh," may answer together with them until the end; see the Shulchan Aruch of the Gaon Rabbeinu Zalman, of blessed memory, siman 109, se'if 5.

clarification.explanation: An individual praying who did not hear "Nakdishach" from the chazan himself, but heard the congregation answering "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" — may join in answering with them until the end.
takeaways: Even without hearing the chazan's opening, one may join in answering the Kedushah upon hearing the congregation answer.

paragraphs: If a person finished his prayer before the chazan finished [his silent Amidah], he should not converse, and should not study even words of Torah, between the silent prayer and the repetition, but rather should stand and be silent and wait until the chazan begins the repetition, and should direct his attention to hearing the repetition from beginning to end; he should not study during the repetition, and certainly should not converse. He must stand on his feet until the end of the repetition and not sit — except an elderly person, or one who is sick and very weak, for whom standing is difficult, in which case he may sit. And if there are individuals who prolong their prayer, the chazan does not wait for them — but only if they prolong excessively; however, if they do not prolong much, but rather pray word by word [at a normal pace], he must wait for them. And if it happens that one who is a great Torah scholar prolongs his prayer, and sees that the chazan is waiting for him, he is permitted to take three steps back immediately after saying the first "Yihyu LeRatzon," so that the chazan can begin the repetition, and then finish "Elohai Netzor" and the other supplications that he customarily says before "Oseh Shalom," at the end of his steps.

clarification.explanation: One who finished his prayer before the chazan should not converse and should not study (even Torah) between the silent prayer and the repetition, but rather should stand, be silent, and wait for the repetition to begin, directing his attention to hear it in its entirety from beginning to end. He must stand on his feet throughout the repetition (except an elderly or sick person, who may sit). If individuals prolong their prayer excessively, the chazan does not wait for them; but if they do not prolong much, he waits. A great Torah scholar who sees that the chazan is waiting for him may take three steps back after the first "Yihyu LeRatzon" so as to allow the chazan to begin, and finish his remaining supplications at the end of his steps.
takeaways: One who finishes his prayer before the chazan remains silent and directs his attention to the entire repetition, standing.
The chazan waits for those who prolong their prayer only within reasonable measure.

paragraphs: When a person hears the mention of [God's] Name in any berachah, he should say "Baruch Hu U'varuch Shemo" ("Blessed is He and blessed is His Name"), and at the end of the berachah he must be careful to answer "Amen" properly. And for any berachah of praise, the intention of the Amen is to mean "true" (emet) — that is, the Amen of the first three berachot [of the Amidah], their intention is "emet." And for the other berachot of the prayer, which contain both praise and petition, there are two intentions in the Amen: he intends "emet," and also intends "may it be [His] will" (ken yehi ratzon). And there are those who say that even in the two berachot "Magen Avraham" and "Mechayeh Hameitim" [within the first three], one should intend both [meanings], and only in "Ha'El HaKadosh" does one intend "emet" [alone].

clarification.explanation: One who hears the mention of God's Name in any berachah says "Baruch Hu U'varuch Shemo," and answers "Amen" properly at its conclusion. The meaning of the "Amen" changes depending on the berachah: in the first three berachot (Avot, Gevurot, Kedushat HaShem), which are [purely] praise, the intention of the Amen is "emet" alone; while in the other berachot of the prayer, which contain both praise and petition, the intention of the Amen is twofold — both "emet" and "ken yehi ratzon." And there are those who say that even in two of the first three berachot themselves — "Magen Avraham" (the closing of the berachah of Avot) and "Mechayeh Hameitim" (the closing of the berachah of Gevurot) — one should intend both meanings together (emet and also ken yehi ratzon), and only in the berachah of "Ha'El HaKadosh" (the closing of the berachah of Kedushat HaShem) does the intention remain "emet" alone according to all opinions.
takeaways: The intention of the "Amen" changes according to the type of berachah: praise alone (emet), or praise and petition together (emet plus ken yehi ratzon).

There are those who say that even in "Magen Avraham" and "Mechayeh Hameitim" (though among the first three berachot) one should intend both meanings together, and only in "Ha'El HaKadosh" is the intention "emet" alone.

paragraphs: One should not answer Amen after the chazan has [already] begun the second berachah, but should answer immediately upon the chazan's conclusion of the berachah. And if the chazan is quick and races like a deer, such that immediately upon concluding the berachah he begins the one after it, one should not answer Amen [at all] — and the penalty is upon the chazan, as mentioned in the Acharonim.

clarification.explanation: One should not answer Amen after the chazan has already begun the next berachah, but should answer immediately upon its conclusion. A chazan who rushes too much (moving immediately to the next berachah) bears the penalty for it, not the congregation.
takeaways: One answers Amen immediately upon the conclusion of the berachah; a chazan who rushes excessively bears the responsibility.

paragraphs: One should not answer a "snatched Amen" (amen chatufah) — that is, before the one reciting the berachah has finished — nor a "clipped Amen" (amen ketufah), such as when the alef is vocalized with a sheva. The same law applies that one should not say it with a shuruk or cholam vowel, for then it would not carry the meaning of affirmation. Nor should it be "ketufah" in the sense of omitting the nun, so that it is not pronounced clearly and distinctly. Likewise, one should not say "Amanei" as if adding a yud. Nor should one answer an "orphaned Amen" (amen yetomah), where he does not know which berachah is being recited — however, if he heard its conclusion, namely "Baruch Atah Hashem, Magen Avraham," and likewise with the others, that suffices for him to answer Amen. And all this law regarding an "orphaned Amen" applies only to a berachah in which this person is obligated, since he is praying it together with them; but if he is not obligated in it, since he is not praying that prayer together with them, as soon as he hears them answering Amen he may answer with them; see the Acharonim, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: One should not answer an "amen chatufah" (before the one reciting the blessing has finished), nor an "amen ketufah" (with a distorted vocalization or pronunciation that loses the meaning), nor "amanei" (adding a yud), nor an "amen yetomah" (without knowing which berachah is being recited). If he heard only the conclusion of the berachah (such as "Magen Avraham"), that suffices to answer. This rule applies specifically to one who is praying with the congregation in that same prayer; one who is not praying with them, and merely hears them answering Amen, may answer regardless.
takeaways: One should avoid an "amen chatufah/ketufah/yetomah" — answering precisely and at the right time.

paragraphs: One who answers Amen should not raise his voice louder than the one reciting the berachah, and he must pay attention to the voice of the one reciting the berachah, so that he answers with a voice measure for measure [matching it].

clarification.explanation: One who answers Amen should not raise his voice above that of the one reciting the berachah, but should match the volume of his own voice to it.
takeaways: One answers Amen at a volume that does not exceed the voice of the one reciting the berachah.

paragraphs: When the chazan reaches "Modim," the congregation bows together with him, but they should not bow excessively — only a bowing of the head. And if an individual is standing in his own prayer, he should be silent and bow silently together with the congregation when they bow at the word "Modim." And there are people who, in their innocence, lose out on answering Amen to "HaMachazir Shechinato LeTzion" because of their haste to bow at "Modim" — therefore a person should pay attention to this, to answer Amen [first], and only afterward bow at the word "Modim."

clarification.explanation: When the chazan reaches "Modim," the congregation bows together with him — a bowing of the head only, without exaggeration. An individual praying silently should also bow silently together with the congregation. There are those who mistakenly lose out on answering Amen to "HaMachazir Shechinato LeTzion" due to their haste to bow at "Modim" — one must be careful to answer Amen first, and only then bow at "Modim."
takeaways: One bows at "Modim" (a bowing of the head only), but only after answering Amen to "HaMachazir Shechinato LeTzion."

paragraphs: People who did not have a complete minyan and were compelled to stand and pray in another place individually, and while they were praying, other people joined them who also stood to pray, and when they finished, they found that they had a complete minyan among them — according to the Radbaz, of blessed memory, they cannot [now] recite the repetition, since each person prayed individually by himself, and Kaddish, Kedushah, and the repetition of that prayer have flown away from them; and even though afterward they found themselves joined together and standing in the place of a complete minyan, they cannot recite the repetition, Kedushah, and "Kaddish Titkabel." This is the opposite of the words of Maran, of blessed memory, in siman 69:1, and as "Dagul MeRevavah" wrote, and in my holy books "Rav Pe'alim" I raised this: although we generally rely on [the ruling of] Maran, nevertheless in such a case, since there is a doubt regarding berachot, we are concerned for the opinion of the Radbaz and those who agree with him. However, although they should not say "Kaddish Titkabel," they may nonetheless say "Kaddish Yehe Shelama" after the Psalms, and also "Kaddish Al Yisrael" and "Barchu" that are said after "Pittum HaKetoret."

clarification.explanation: People who did not have a complete minyan and prayed individually in the same place, and afterward others joined them and a complete minyan formed — according to the Radbaz, they cannot now say Kaddish, Kedushah, and the repetition of that prayer, since each of them already prayed individually. Although in principle we rely on Maran (who permits this), because of the doubt regarding berachot we are concerned for the opinion of the Radbaz, and therefore they do not say "Kaddish Titkabel" (which belongs to the repetition) — but they may say "Kaddish Yehe Shelama" after the Psalms, as well as "Kaddish Al Yisrael" and "Barchu" said after "Pittum HaKetoret."
takeaways: A minyan that formed only after each person had already prayed individually does not say "Kaddish Titkabel" (out of doubt), but does say other forms of Kaddish (Yehe Shelama, Al Yisrael).
